name: Saw palmetto
lead: Saw palmetto (Serenoa repens) is a small palm native to the subtropical southeastern United States and Mexico. Extracts of its berries are sold as supplements for prostate symptoms and, increasingly, for hair loss [1][2]. It is among the botanical products promoted as natural DHT blockers because extracts have antiandrogenic properties in laboratory studies [3][4].

Published reviews of saw palmetto in hair loss describe a small number of trials. A 2020 systematic review identified five randomised trials and two cohort studies reporting positive effects of oral and topical saw palmetto-containing supplements in androgenetic alopecia and telogen effluvium, while noting that robust high-quality data are lacking [3]. More recent industry-linked randomised trials of proprietary extracts in self-perceived thinning hair have been published [5][6][7].

For prostate symptoms, Wikipedia reports that as of 2023 there is no scientific evidence that the extract is effective for benign prostatic hyperplasia or cancer, though an earlier review of one standardised extract found it may relieve urinary symptoms [1]. Reviews of herb-drug interactions place saw palmetto among supplements with a low likelihood of drug interactions [8], and a bleeding review did not associate it with bleeding [9].

paras: Saw palmetto is taken orally or applied topically in products for male and female pattern hair loss and self-perceived thinning. Reviews of natural products for androgenetic alopecia include saw palmetto among candidates, alongside caffeine, melatonin, rosemary oil and pumpkin seed oil, based on small clinical studies [10][11].

The extract is widely used for lower urinary tract symptoms from benign prostatic hyperplasia. Reviews list it among herbal drugs used for that condition [12]. Trials include a US phase 3 study and several others registered on ClinicalTrials.gov [13][14][15].

Hair: the 2020 systematic review summarised effects such as a 60 percent improvement in overall hair quality, a 27 percent improvement in total hair count, increased density in 83.3 percent of patients and stabilised progression in 52 percent across various saw palmetto-containing supplements, with no serious adverse events, while calling for larger trials [3]. These products often contained other ingredients.

A 2023 double-blind placebo-controlled study randomised 80 men and women aged 18 to 50 with mild-to-moderate androgenetic alopecia to a standardised saw palmetto oil (2 to 3 percent beta-sitosterol) in oral or topical forms, or placebo, over 16 weeks, and reported reduced hair fall and improved growth [5]. Two further randomised trials of proprietary extracts in adults with self-perceived thinning hair reported 90-day and 180-day results [6][7]. These studies were of branded ingredients and the abstracts available here do not give effect sizes.
A systematic review and network meta-analysis of dietary supplements for androgenetic alopecia has also been published [16].
Prostate: a 2000 randomised trial and literature search, a 2024 uroflowmetry trial and the CAMUS and PERLES studies examined saw palmetto and related extracts for urinary symptoms [14][15][17][18].

Trials in alopecia reported good tolerability [3]. A review of herbal supplement-drug interactions classed saw palmetto with those having low likelihood of interactions with most medications [8]. A bleeding review found no association with bleeding [9]. A 1999 laboratory study examined inhibition of human sperm motility by several herbs, including saw palmetto [19].

Extracts contain fatty acids and phytosterols and are described as inhibiting 5-alpha-reductase and possibly androgen receptor binding; reviews attribute these antiandrogenic properties as the rationale for hair and prostate use [3][4][12].
Indigenous peoples of the southeastern US used the fruit and fibres, and the fruit was historically a food [1]. Saw palmetto was discussed in a medical journal as early as 1912 [20].
